items.followUp: Write the reactions of chlorine and bromine with water.

rubric.why: Checks the balanced reaction of fluorine with water.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction of fluorine with water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct balanced equation.

rubric.why: Checks that another halogen reacts with water to form a hydrogen halide and a hypohalous acid.
rubric.description: Writes a correct reaction of chlorine, bromine, or iodine with water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct equation; a reversible arrow is acceptable.

modelAnswer: Fluorine reacts vigorously with water: 2F₂ + 2H₂O → 4HF + O₂.
Chlorine reacts reversibly with water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO.
Bromine reacts reversibly with water: Br₂ + H₂O ⇌ HBr + HBrO.
Iodine reacts only slightly with water: I₂ + H₂O ⇌ HI + HIO.

items.followUp: State any four postulates of Bohr’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Checks the basic arrangement of electrons around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the nucleus and electrons revolving around it.

rubric.why: Checks that electrons can occupy only certain allowed paths or levels.
rubric.description: States that electrons occupy permitted circular orbits, shells, or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the restricted or fixed nature of the electron orbits or levels.

rubric.why: Checks that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-energy postulate.

rubric.why: Checks that electrons in permitted orbits do not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate or lose energy while in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-radiation postulate.

rubric.why: Checks how electrons change energy when moving between levels.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs or emits energy when it moves between energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the transition and associated energy change.

modelAnswer: An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons revolve around it.
Electrons can revolve only in certain permitted circular orbits, called shells or energy levels.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate or lose energy while they remain in a permitted orbit.
An electron absorbs or emits energy when it moves between energy levels; the energy change is ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Classify mixtures into homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks that a mixture contains multiple substances combined physically.
rubric.description: Defines a mixture as two or more substances physically combined.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both that it contains two or more substances and that they are physically combined.

rubric.why: Checks that mixture components retain their properties or can be separated physically.
rubric.description: States that the components retain their properties or can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either key feature.

rubric.why: Checks the homogeneous class and an appropriate example.
rubric.description: Identifies a homogeneous mixture as uniform throughout and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the classification, its uniform nature, and a suitable example.

rubric.why: Checks the heterogeneous class and an appropriate example.
rubric.description: Identifies a heterogeneous mixture as non-uniform and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the classification, its non-uniform nature, and a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances in any proportion; its components retain their properties and can be separated by physical methods.
A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; examples include salt water and air.
A heterogeneous mixture does not have a uniform composition throughout; examples include oil and water or sand and water.

items.followUp: Define metallic bonding and draw a labelled diagram showing the arrangement of particles in a metal.

rubric.why: Checks that the definition identifies the two particles involved in metallic bonding.
rubric.description: Identifies positive metal ions and delocalised or mobile electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both types of particles.

rubric.why: Checks the nature of the force that constitutes the metallic bond.
rubric.description: Defines the metallic bond as the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the electrostatic attraction between the ions and electrons.

rubric.why: Checks the arrangement of the metal ions.
rubric.description: Explains that positive metal ions are arranged in a regular lattice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the regular lattice of positive ions.

rubric.why: Checks that the electrons are free to move through the structure.
rubric.description: Explains that delocalised electrons move throughout the lattice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the mobile or delocalised electrons.

rubric.why: Checks that the diagram represents and labels both parts of the metallic structure.
rubric.description: Provides a labelled diagram showing positive ions and mobile electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear diagram with both particle types labelled.

modelAnswer: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons surrounding them.
The metal atoms release their outer electrons, which become delocalised and move throughout the structure.
The positive ions remain arranged in a regular lattice, and the attraction between them and the mobile electrons holds the metal together.
Diagram:
M⁺       M⁺       M⁺   ← positive metal ions
e⁻  e⁻  e⁻  e⁻      ← delocalised, mobile electrons
M⁺       M⁺       M⁺   ← positive metal ions

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and explain how temperature and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of vapour pressure under equilibrium conditions.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including pressure due to vapour and equilibrium with the liquid.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Explains that vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: Checks how the strength of intermolecular forces affects vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Explains that weaker intermolecular forces give higher vapour pressure, while stronger forces give lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between intermolecular forces and vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of a dissolved non-volatile solute.
rubric.description: States that a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of a liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container at a given temperature.
As temperature increases, more liquid molecules escape into the vapour phase, so vapour pressure increases.
The nature of the liquid affects its vapour pressure: weaker intermolecular forces give a higher vapour pressure, while stronger forces give a lower vapour pressure.
A dissolved non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid.

items.followUp: Define a diatomic molecule and give two examples other than nitrogen and oxygen.

rubric.why: Checks the defining number of atoms in a diatomic molecule.
rubric.description: Defines a diatomic molecule as a molecule containing two atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a molecule contains two atoms.

rubric.why: Checks that two suitable examples are given.
rubric.description: Gives two correct examples of diatomic molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct examples.

modelAnswer: A diatomic molecule is a molecule made up of two atoms.
Examples include H₂ and O₂.
